gaps.question: The paper evaluates the predicates by lazy determinization of the finite-state transducer, following Snæbjarnarson et al. (2026), and gives no further detail. How is this done? There is_cylinder == is_member because the codon output only grows, so in this setup no remainder entries ever arise (member implies cylinder) and R stays empty. Is that right?

gaps.question: Neither prune_M nor prune_tau says how equal weights are ordered by sort_descending, nor whether prune_tau compares W_i >= (1-tau)W_N with exact or tolerant floating-point comparison. How is this done? We assumed: Use a stable descending sort by weight (ties keep insertion order, e.g. numpy argsort(-w, kind='stable')) and an exact >= comparison on cumulative sums computed in that order. In the worst case all covering particles have equal weight, so any tie rule gives the same total min(M, 3^T) * 4^(-3T) (Eq. 49 with equality); tie order only changes which strings are kept. Is that right?
gaps.assumption: Use a stable descending sort by weight (ties keep insertion order, e.g. numpy argsort(-w, kind='stable')) and an exact >= comparison on cumulative sums computed in that order. In the worst case all covering particles have equal weight, so any tie rule gives the same total min(M, 3^T) * 4^(-3T) (Eq. 49 with equality); tie order only changes which strings are kept.

gaps.question: The paper does not say how to handle floating-point error in pps/systematic: sum(pi) may differ from M by rounding, and pi_i may land just below 1 for a particle that should be pinned. How is this done? We assumed: Compute pi in float64; after pps, clip pi to [0,1]; in systematic use u + k for k = 0..M-1 against the cumulative sums and take exactly M (or m) indices via searchsorted on C (side='right'), rescaling C so that C_N = M exactly. Return exactly M distinct survivors whenever |I+| > M. Is that right?
gaps.assumption: Compute pi in float64; after pps, clip pi to [0,1]; in systematic use u + k for k = 0..M-1 against the cumulative sums and take exactly M (or m) indices via searchsorted on C (side='right'), rescaling C so that C_N = M exactly. Return exactly M distinct survivors whenever |I+| > M.

gaps.question: Fig. 10 stops a particle only when it samples EOS; it has no cylinder check. In the worst case of setup.py the source never emits EOS (UNIFORM has p(EOS|x) = 0 everywhere), so q(EOS|x) = 0, the weight stays constant once the prefix covers y, the tail roulette never fires, and smc_simple as written never halts. The paper's App. E source instead puts all mass on strings of length exactly 3T. How is this done? We assumed: Follow Fig. 10 as written: no cylinder shortcut. Particles stop only by sampling EOS. Both sources in setup.py stop with probability one (bigram: 0.02 after each base; worst case: exactly at length 300, as in App. E), so smc_simple halts without it. Adding the shortcut would turn smc_simple into smc_rb. (Updated by the controller after the yardstick review: setup.UNIFORM now stops at 300.). Is that right?
gaps.assumption: Follow Fig. 10 as written: no cylinder shortcut. Particles stop only by sampling EOS. gaps.question: The paper says the fixed-M methods of Tab. 1 compose their prune with the tail roulette and its halting analysis covers prune_M, but it never states whether the beam_summing + prune_M baseline (or beam_summing + prune_tau) is run with the decorator. How is this done? We assumed: Run beam_summing (prune_M and prune_tau) without the decorator so it stays deterministic, matching Fig. 1 and the 'beam search' framing. In this setup it never matters: each target-prefix call extends a particle at most 3 source symbols before it becomes a cylinder, so weights never fall below e^-30 w0. Is that right?
gaps.assumption: Run beam_summing (prune_M and prune_tau) without the decorator so it stays deterministic, matching Fig. 1 and the 'beam search' framing. In this setup it never matters: each target-prefix call extends a particle at most 3 source symbols before it becomes a cylinder, so weights never fall below e^-30 w0.

gaps.question: Table 1 gives the particle-count column: beam_summing (no prune) unbounded; + prune_M fixed M; + prune_tau mass-set (no M); smc_simple and smc_rb fixed M (M initial particles of weight 1/M); beam_swor fixed M (cap per prune); beam_swor_adaptive adaptive m <= M ('nominal' M). The paper does not say what to report for prune_tau at a given M. What did you use? We assumed: beam_summing with prune_tau ignores M: run it once per target and copy the value into every M and seed slot (Fig. 9a draws it as a flat line). For prune_M, M is the beam width. For smc_simple/smc_rb, M is the initial particle count (pool size is never increased; resampling keeps the current size). For beam_swor M caps survivors per prune; for beam_swor_adaptive it is the maximum in Eq. 16. Is that right?

gaps.question: The paper reports results over S seeds (8 for Table 2, 64 for Fig. 9a) but does not describe its random number generator, how seeds map to runs, or whether runs for different M or targets share randomness. What did you use? We assumed: One independent run per (target i, M index j, seed k) drawing all randomness from setup.rng(i, j, k) (numpy default_rng([seed, i, j])). Deterministic methods (beam_summing) fill every seed slot with the same value. For systematic sampling draw the permutation and u from that generator; for Bernoulli/categorical draws likewise. Is that right?
gaps.assumption: One independent run per (target i, M index j, seed k) drawing all randomness from setup.rng(i, j, k) (numpy default_rng([seed, i, j])). Deterministic methods (beam_summing) fill every seed slot with the same value. For systematic sampling draw the permutation and u from that generator; for Bernoulli/categorical draws likewise.

gaps.question: The paper does not say what an implementation should do when every particle dies (a prune or roulette empties the pool before any quotient mass is collected, or a later target-prefix call starts from an empty quotient). Figs. 7-8 only say a failed GPT-2 run contributes Z_hat_s = 0 to the seed average. What happens here? We assumed: Follow the pseudocode literally: an empty Q' gives an empty starting pool, the while loop does not run, A = 0 (plus any re-checked remainder mass), and the recursion continues to |y|. A final Z_hat of 0 is reported as log_z = -inf (never NaN); the seed average then includes a zero, as in Figs. 7-8. Particles with nu(x) = 0 or lambda(x) = 0 are dropped (Fig. 12 line 129). Is that right?
gaps.assumption: Follow the pseudocode literally: an empty Q' gives an empty starting pool, the while loop does not run, A = 0 (plus any re-checked remainder mass), and the recursion continues to |y|. A final Z_hat of 0 is reported as log_z = -inf (never NaN); the seed average then includes a zero, as in Figs. 7-8. Particles with nu(x) = 0 or lambda(x) = 0 are dropped (Fig. 12 line 129).

gaps.question: The DNA bigram source p_bigram for f_dna2aa is trained on 'the DNA training corpus', which is not named, and its probabilities (including stop probabilities) are not given. p_dna is a GPT-2 model trained on human DNA (Snæbjarnarson et al. 2026). What did you use? We assumed: Use setup.BIGRAM, a hand-set high-entropy, A/T-rich, CpG-depleted bigram over ACGT with start row (.30,.20,.20,.30, no stop) and stop probability 0.02 after every base (high enough that smc_simple, which walks each particle to EOS, fits the time budget). It is a stand-in, so Table 2's DNA numbers are not reproducible; we test the claims (unbiased, error falls with M, beam_summing is a lower bound). p_dna (GPT-2 on DNA) is not covered. Is that right?

gaps.question: f_dna2aa maps DNA strings over a four-letter alphabet to amino-acid strings, each amino acid being the image of several codons. The paper does not give the codon table, reading frame, handling of stop codons, or what a trailing partial codon emits. How is this done? We assumed: setup.CodonTransducer: standard genetic code, frame 0, codons read left to right; each complete codon emits one amino acid; the three stop codons (TAA, TAG, TGA) emit '*' and do not terminate the output; a trailing partial codon emits nothing. is_member(x,y) = output(x) starts with y; is_cylinder = is_member; is_live also accepts a partial final codon that some codon for the next target symbol extends. Is that right?
gaps.assumption: setup.CodonTransducer: standard genetic code, frame 0, codons read left to right; each complete codon emits one amino acid; the three stop codons (TAA, TAG, TGA) emit '*' and do not terminate the output; a trailing partial codon emits nothing. is_member(x,y) = output(x) starts with y; is_cylinder = is_member; is_live also accepts a partial final codon that some codon for the next target symbol extends.

gaps.question: App. E's source puts all mass on strings of length exactly 3T (so it stops with probability one after 3T symbols), but the paper does not spell out the stop rule as a next-symbol model. What did you use? We assumed: setup.UNIFORM gives 1/4 per base and stops after exactly 300 bases (p(EOS|x) = 1 at length 300, 0 before), matching App. E's p_X(x) = (1/4)^{3T} over strings of length 3T. The worst case also turns the tail roulette off (kappa = 0): the decomposition is finite, so every method halts, and the paper's exactness argument ignores the roulette. setup.py adds a second worst-case target (WORST_MIX) made of amino acids whose codons share their first two bases, where the same argument holds. Is that right?
